in_context.text: This verse ends Paul's list of qualities for a bishop, an overseer of the church (3:1-7). After character, family life, and maturity, he adds one more test: people outside the church must think well of him. Otherwise he may be disgraced and caught in the devil's trap.

speaker.text: Paul the apostle is writing. He names himself at the start of the letter. Many critical scholars think a follower wrote in his name.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, whom Paul left to lead the church at Ephesus.

affected.text: The man who would serve as bishop (overseer) in the church. The verse also concerns how 'them which are without', people outside the church, see him.

what.text: A church leader must have a good reputation among non-believers. Without it, he risks falling into public disgrace and into a snare set by the devil.

events.text: Paul gives this instruction while Timothy is leading the Ephesian church and Paul is away, hoping to come soon (3:14).

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, between Paul's two Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110, though others defend the earlier date.

where.text: The church was in Ephesus. It was a wealthy port and capital of the Roman province of Asia, known for its temple of Artemis. Where Paul wrote from is not stated, perhaps Macedonia.

purpose.text: Paul writes so Timothy will know how people should behave in God's household, the church (3:15). Choosing leaders of proven character is part of that.

big_picture.text: The letter teaches that belief and behavior belong together. Elsewhere Paul urges believers to walk wisely and honestly 'toward them that are without', so the church is not blamed.

for_readers.text: A leader's life is seen by outsiders, not just by the church. A bad public name harms the leader and the church's witness.

why_it_matters.text: 'Them which are without' means outsiders, people not in the church. Paul uses similar wording elsewhere for how believers should act toward non-believers.
The word means witness or testimony. A 'good report' is the good witness others give about the man, much like the 'honest report' required in Acts 6:3.
This is a trap. The same image appears in 1 Timothy 6:9 and 2 Timothy 2:26, where people are taken captive in the devil's snare.
The word literally means slanderer or false accuser. One lexicon notes it could be read here as human slanderers, though it usually means the Devil.

takeaway.text: Church leaders should be people whom even outsiders respect. A bad public name invites disgrace and spiritual danger, and it hurts the church's witness.

unsupported.reason: Only 2 Timothy 2:26 speaks of being taken captive in the devil's snare. 1 Timothy 6:9 mentions a snare for those who want to be rich, but it does not mention the devil or captivity.
